2	
3	## Destination and core question
4	
5	- **B-01 — Destination.** An MCP tool for discussing books with Claude: the author reads on his iPhone and wants to talk with an LLM about the book he is reading, its last chapter, and the highlights made since the last conversation. CLI first, deliberately — the author knows CLI design and TDD/BDD cold, while MCP was unfamiliar territory; the CLI is the walking skeleton of the broader vision.
6	- **B-02 — Core question.** Can an LLM be a good pair programmer? The author had no colleagues to pair with; this project is the experiment. The method is the point: executable specifications nail verifiable invariants, and the art is slicing the problem and designing specs with minimal coupling to implementation — London school, GOOS lineage. The root principle everything else derives from: the spec's job is nailing requirements in a falsifiable way. Executable specification, GOOS layers, enforced layer separation, and delegation contracts all follow from falsifiability — a hierarchy, not parallel motivations.
7	- **B-03 — Why Apple Books as testbed.** Deliberately chosen because the Apple Books database schema is undocumented and evolves with each macOS release. That makes the project a test of long-term software evolution and maintenance — the opposite of one-shotting problems the model already knows from pretraining.
8	- **B-04 — Book-grounding motivation (product feeds process).** Pretrained simulacra of TDD/BDD experts proved shallow caricatures — skewed, non-actionable summaries of real positions. A core BookMinder motivation is giving the model access to full books as consultation material, so actionable principles can be extracted from primary sources that did not survive pretraining summarization. The failure-mode name for the thing this defeats: simulacra-shallowness.
9	- **B-05 — The project is a vehicle and a benchmark.** The real object of study is whether an AI coding agent can hold a strict ATDD process as a pair programmer; process artifacts are therefore deliverables, not cruft. 9	## Session-transcript preservation
10	
11	- **B-32 — Native transcript backup (cloud/ephemeral containers only).** `claude-dev-log-diary/jsonl/` preserves full session transcripts in the agentic system's native format — the machine-readable source the day-files only shadow; layout and copy commands live in its README. When working in an ephemeral container (Claude Code cloud infra), the container's transcript dies with it, so snapshot the session's `.jsonl` file + directory from the harness project store (`/root/.claude/projects/<project>/`) into `jsonl/cloud-<year>/` and commit: (1) always toward session end, when the final branch push is being prepared; (2) incrementally at natural stable points — after a major phase of work lands, or when resuming after a long pause (the pause's tail is then on disk). Copies are append-only extensions, so re-snapshotting is always safe; batch the snapshot into an adjacent commit rather than making high-frequency snapshot-only commits. A transcript cannot contain its own final minutes — the true tail of a session is captured by the next session's first snapshot. Local (non-ephemeral) sessions are exempt: the harness store persists there, and the author owns backup timing.

13	## Backlog and stories
14	
15	- **B-23 — Backlog practice.** Stories are YAML cards under `stories/` in story-map columns: `discover` covers listing, filtering, admin access, and error handling; `access` is controlling the Apple Books app; `review` is highlights and notes; `export` is text extraction. Every card carries a mandatory `status` from the vocabulary CLAUDE.md `<backlog_management>` defines — status only, no priority/assignee metadata (YAGNI). TODO.md's Discover Column is a bare list of story paths in implementation order: the order is the plan, so take the next story in order rather than offering a menu, and keep the list free of emoji, numbering, and per-item rationale. Completed Features is an immutable record of the journey — never reorder or remove entries; annotate a reopened story in place (`[REOPENED: ...]`); refactorings are not listed there (user-visible stories only); a doc deletion gets a one-line breadcrumb with its commit hash. 17	## Settled design decisions in the code
18	
19	- **B-24 — CLI shape.** `main` is a Click group; `list` is a subgroup declared `@main.group(name="list")` on a function named `list_cmd` — never name the function `list`, which shadows the builtin and breaks `list[Book]` annotations at import time (fix name collisions at the source, not with deprecated typing aliases). Subcommands `recent` and `all` share options via the `with_common_list_options` decorator (Click does not inherit group options). Filter vocabulary: one repeatable `--filter` option whose values are attribute names with `!` negation (`cloud`, `!cloud`, `sample`, `!sample`) — `!` and not `-` because Click parses a leading `-` as an option; filters are orthogonal to list commands (nothing in Apple Books' UI makes them command-specific). `list recent` deliberately replicates Apple's Continue section so that an agent consuming the future MCP surface and the human looking at the app share one frame of reference. `--user` is simultaneously a real admin feature (examine another user's books) and the test seam — the admin use case is what licenses it in production. 20	- **B-25 — The Book type.** One `Book` TypedDict with `NotRequired` optional fields; never a parallel type for a variant that adds a field. Only `title` and `author` are required — `path` and `updated` are `NotRequired` because the SQLite path cannot supply them (see domain page). TypedDict is a static annotation only: it produces a plain dict, no attribute access, no runtime key enforcement.

22	## Fixture architecture
23	
24	- **B-26 — Synthetic $HOME personas and the front-door seam.** Integration fixtures are synthetic home-directory trees under `specs/apple_books/fixtures/users/<persona>/` replicating Apple's container layout path-for-path. Each persona encodes a container state observed on a real machine: `test_reader` (full library), `fresh_books_user` (all containers, empty plist, empty-schema sqlite), `legacy_books_user` (containers but no BKLibrary directory), `never_opened_user` (only the OS-created `com.apple.iBooksX` container — no BKAgentService, no plist, no sqlite), `corrupted_db_user` (zero-byte plist and sqlite; note a corruption scenario needs the full container present or the plist check fires before the sqlite error). The seam is the front door: `--user` with an absolute path is used verbatim as the home directory, a bare name resolves to `/Users/<name>`, `None` to `Path.home()` — exactly three cases, specced in `library._get_user_path`, no falsy-string case. Specs must pass absolute fixture paths (a relative path is treated as a username and silently rewritten). This seam exists because fixtures through the product's own parameter exercise the real path-construction code, where patching a private module name would bypass it; the older module-constant seam (`BKLIBRARY_DB_FILE`-style) survives only with its known limitation — it is an in-process substitution resolved at import time and cannot cross a subprocess boundary.
25	- **B-27 — Fixture data discipline.** The fixture database carries the real schema verbatim — dump `.schema ZBKLIBRARYASSET` from a live database, never hand-write a schema. Prefer extending `test_reader` over new personas unless a test needs isolation. After any fixture change, verify through the product: `python -m bookminder list recent --user <absolute fixture path>`.

This cloud environment has no live Apple Books library, so any exploration here runs against fixtures only: say so explicitly and mark conclusions provisional. Fixtures freeze time — any recency-window behavior must be specified with controlled time, or the snapshot silently ages out of the window.

2	
3	Verification status is honest here: **verified@tree** = encoded in the current code/fixtures and exercised by the suite; **observed-2025** = established against a live library in 2025, needs a fresh live-DB probe before you lean on it; **hypothesis** = open, never settled. This environment has no live Apple Books database — nothing here can be re-verified in place, only against fixtures.
4	
5	## Data sources
6	
7	- **B-40 — Two sandboxed containers (verified@tree, encoded at library.py:17-25).** `~/Library/Containers/com.apple.BKAgentService/Data/Documents/iBooks/Books/` holds `Books.plist` (the catalogue) beside per-book `<numeric-id>.epub` items. `~/Library/Containers/com.apple.iBooksX/Data/Documents/BKLibrary/` holds the library database. Discover the database by glob — `BKLibrary-*.sqlite` — never by literal filename: the numeric segments (e.g. `BKLibrary-1-091020131601.sqlite`) are per-install artifacts.
8	- **B-41 — Plist vs database roles (observed-2025; the split is load-bearing for the whole design).** `Books.plist` is a catalogue: `itemName`, `artistName`, `path`, `updateDate`. Its `BKPercentComplete` appears only on finished books (always 1.0) — it cannot express in-progress reading. Real reading state lives in the database table `ZBKLIBRARYASSET` (`ZREADINGPROGRESS`, `ZLASTOPENDATE`, `ZISFINISHED`, `ZDATEFINISHED`, `ZCREATIONDATE`). The database is the authoritative catalogue: the plist omits cloud-only titles, so absence from the plist proves nothing about library membership, and a title's absence is never evidence of cloud status. `updateDate` in the plist is publisher-revision metadata, not reading activity — BookMinder cares about the user's relationship to the book, which lives in the database. Books lazy-download from iCloud: a book in the catalogue with no file on disk is a valid library entry — never filter books by on-disk file existence.
9	- **B-42 — Apple epoch (verified@tree, library.py:11,65-66).** Core Data timestamps count seconds from 2001-01-01 UTC, not 1970 — raw values look like plausible Unix times and are silently ~31 years wrong without the `APPLE_EPOCH` offset.
10	
11	## The ZSTATE census — the project's signature reflex
12	
13	- **B-43 — ZSTATE is a small enum whose census must be re-taken, not recalled.** Every single-value story ever told about ZSTATE ("5 means cloud", "5 means series", "3 is the cloud value") was contradicted by the next batch of real rows; books showing the UI cloud icon were observed at ZSTATE 1, 3, and 6. The working set the code encodes (observed-2025, at library.py:76-77): **1** = present locally (including downloaded samples), **3** = cloud book, **6** = cloud sample not yet downloaded. **ZSTATE 5 is an OPEN HYPOTHESIS, not a verified mapping**: earlier research recorded it as "Series entity / unowned series book" (linked by ZSERIESID, with the entity's ZTITLE being the series name), and `docs/apple_books.md` still asserts that as verified — but a later systematic re-probe observed 5 only as a *second* row for a title that already had a 3, which the series story does not predict. Until a live-DB re-census settles it, treat 5 as unmapped and the docs' "Verified ZSTATE Mappings" section as over-claiming. The method that produced every real breakthrough here: enumerate all distinct values DB-first and characterize each, instead of reasoning UI-first from the values already seen.
14	- **B-44 — Sample detection is a composite predicate (verified@tree, library.py:77).** `is_sample` = `ZSTATE = 6 OR ZISSAMPLE = 1`. `ZISSAMPLE = 0` is never proof a book is not a sample — unmistakable UI samples carried `ZISSAMPLE = 0` and were identifiable only by `ZSTATE = 6`. Lifecycle (hypothesis, explains the composite): a store sample enters the library as `ZSTATE=6, ZISSAMPLE=0` (cloud sample) and becomes `ZSTATE=1, ZISSAMPLE=1` once opened/downloaded. ZSTATE 6 is the common case, downloaded samples the edge case — cover both. Per-title sample observations flipped between probes in 2025 (the same title read `ZISSAMPLE 0` one session and `1` another), so any per-title claim needs a freshness stamp and a re-run query, never a citation of notes. Cloud display vs cloud filter diverge at HEAD (verified@tree): `is_cloud` = `ZSTATE in (3, 6)` (library.py:76) but `--filter cloud` matches `ZSTATE = 3` only (library.py:154-159) — a cloud sample displays ☁️ yet is excluded by the cloud filter; know this before "fixing" either side without a spec.
15	- **B-45 — ZCONTENTTYPE is unverified (hypothesis).** Likely 1 = book (EPUB), 3 = PDF — hedged until re-verified on a live database. `docs/apple_books.md` states it hedged at line 60 and flat at lines 114-115; the hedged form governs.
16	- **B-46 — Column facts.** `ZTITLE` is not a key (observed-2025): one title can have multiple rows (duplicate rows at different ZSTATEs, even under two author strings), so any title lookup must handle and explain duplicates or detection becomes non-deterministic. `ZISFINISHED = 1` is the sole definition of finished (observed-2025): finished books exist below 100% progress, so never require `ZREADINGPROGRESS = 1.0`. `ZLASTOPENDATE` was never NULL for rows with progress > 0 (observed-2025, 221 rows, 0 nulls) — the basis for not guarding it; re-verify before adding or removing guards.
17	- **B-47 — Samples and `list recent` (hypothesis).** Apple Books appears never to populate `ZREADINGPROGRESS` for samples — a sample's reading position was traced to a type-3 annotation in the AEAnnotation database instead. Since `list recent` filters on `ZREADINGPROGRESS > 0`, sample filtering there is structurally near-empty; library-wide sample listing belongs on `list all`.
18	- **B-48 — "Want to Read" is unresolved (hypothesis).** Composition held as unread-or-sample (`ZREADINGPROGRESS = 0` and not finished, OR sample) for all observed titles, but its ordering was never established — the recorded ZCREATIONDATE conclusion rests on a known arithmetic error. The list is computed by Apple, not marked by the user: document observed database behavior, never inferred user intent, and say "unknown" when the mechanism is unknown.
19	
20	## Environment facts
21	
22	- **B-49 — Container lifecycle (observed-2025 on real machines).** `com.apple.iBooksX` is created at macOS account setup; `com.apple.BKAgentService`, `Books.plist`, and the `BKLibrary-*.sqlite` (with 0 rows) are all created together on first launch of Apple Books — no Apple ID required. Reading another user's `~/Library` requires sudo; a plain `--user <name>` run fails with PermissionError. These states are exactly what the fixture personas encode.
23	- **B-50 — Plist mechanics.** `Books.plist` stores `Books` as an ARRAY of dicts — a dict-keyed-by-id variant parses without error and silently yields zero books (verified@tree: the code guards for list shape, library.py:85-86). Read with `plistlib.load(open(path, "rb"))` — it auto-detects binary and XML; never shell out to `plutil -convert`. For human/agent exploration, render plists as Swift literals: `plutil -convert swift -o out.swift Books.plist` — far more token-efficient than XML; that is what the `All_Books*.swift` dumps are.
24	- **B-51 — Path correlation is an open problem (verified@tree, library.py:73).** The book file path exists only in `Books.plist`; the database has no usable path, so `_row_to_book` sets `path=""` pending a `ZASSETID`-keyed correlation between the two sources. This is acknowledged design debt, not an oversight.
25	
26	## Working the database
27	
28	- **B-52 — Query discipline.** Answer one-off questions with the `sqlite3` CLI directly — no throwaway .py scripts in the tree, no print-debugging through production code. Use targeted column lists, never `SELECT *` (blurb columns flood the context). Parameterize titles with `?` placeholders — hand-escaping apostrophes ("What's Our Problem?") fails repeatedly. When a diacritics-bearing title returns nothing, retry `LIKE` on the longest ASCII-only prefix before concluding the row is absent — the shell round-trip, not the database, is what fails. When probing N items with the same shape, batch with `IN (...)`.
29	- **B-53 — docs/apple_books.md epistemic status.** It is the captured output of the reverse-engineering phase — a running record of guesses about a schema Apple does not document. It is the thing under test, never the reference: verify any attribute row-by-row against the UI screenshots in `docs/ui/apple/` and a live query, never against the doc's own prose. Editing rules the author enforces: the doc stays descriptive of storage (no SQL that prescribes a feature's filtering strategy); every SQL query lives in the single Database-to-UI-Mapping section other sections link to (two copies of one query is how it contradicted itself); UI quirks (cloud samples rendered "1%") are documented but never replicated in the implementation; screenshots are committed into docs/ and referenced inline next to the claims they support, each labelled with the platform that produced it (iPhone tiles and macOS list views use different attribute vocabularies — macOS "Complete" is a long-form percentage, not a status); preserve the section's existing segmentation when updating contents.
